Work is no longer just about earning a living.
The India Health Quotient 2026 measures the Occupational Dimension through factors like work-life balance, career confidence, learning opportunities, workplace relationships, engagement and access to support systems.
India scored 65/100 on the Occupational Dimension.

Key insights:
- 83% prioritise work-life balance
- 63% feel confident about their future career
- 62% stay engaged in work and learning
- Only 43% feel they have access to the resources and support needed to succeed
- Younger Indians aged 25-34 report the lowest occupational wellbeing scores

The findings show that while ambition remains strong, balance has become India's biggest workplace priority.

Health insurance isn't just about paying hospital bills. It's connected to how people experience overall well-being.

This National Insurance Awareness Day, the India Health Quotient 2026 reveals an important insight.
People with health insurance reported a higher overall health score than those without.

The difference goes beyond financial security. Health insurance owners reported stronger scores across all five dimensions of well-being:
✔ Physical
✔ Mental
✔ Financial
✔ Occupational
✔ Social

The report also found:
• 53% worry about unexpected medical expenses
• 50% want protection against future health risks
• 23% have delayed medical treatment because of costs

Yet many people still hesitate to buy health insurance because they feel premiums are expensive or aren't sure which plan to choose.
Insurance awareness isn't just about buying a policy.
It's about making informed decisions that help you stay prepared for life's uncertainties.

Download the India Health Quotient 2026 report.
Link:

The data reveals a gap between managing today and preparing for tomorrow.

The India Health Quotient 2026 reveals an interesting connection between financial wellbeing and health.
41% say chasing financial goals causes stress.
36% say spending on health and wellness can strain their finances.
This creates what we can call the Health Debt Trap: a cycle where financial stress affects health, and health-related expenses add to financial pressure.
The report also found that India's Financial Dimension scored 62/100, the lowest among all five health dimensions. Areas like emergency medical preparedness, future savings and retirement readiness continue to lag behind day-to-day money management.

The takeaway is simple: health and financial wellbeing aren't separate conversations. They're deeply connected.

Download the India Health Quotient 2026 report to explore more insights.
Link:

Drug abuse doesn't always begin with a substance. Sometimes, it begins with stress.
Mental health challenges and substance use are often closely connected.
When stress, anxiety, burnout or isolation go unaddressed, people may turn to unhealthy coping mechanisms in search of relief. But temporary escape is not the same as recovery.

The India Health Quotient 2026 found that 82% of urban Indians report feeling stressed, while 63% say they feel drained, losing enthusiasm, motivation or interest in activities they usually enjoy.
That's why conversations about drug abuse must also include conversations about mental well-being.

This International Day Against Drug Abuse, let's focus on prevention where it starts:
✔️ Recognising stress
✔️ Building healthy coping habits
✔️ Encouraging open conversations
✔️ Seeking support when needed

Because protecting mental health is one of the strongest ways to prevent substance abuse.

For regular health and health insurance updates, join our WhatsApp Channel:

We know how to budget. But are we prepared?
The India Health Quotient 2026 defines the Financial Dimension as a measure of how secure and prepared people feel about their finances today and in the future. It includes budgeting, debt management, emergency preparedness, insurance coverage, savings and retirement planning.

India scored 62/100 on the Financial Dimension, making it the lowest-scoring health dimension in the report.
Key insights:
* Debt and EMI management scored highest (66)
* Budget management followed closely (64)
* Emergency income preparedness and retirement readiness scored lowest (59)
* Adults aged 25-34 recorded the lowest financial health scores
* People with health insurance reported stronger financial preparedness overall

The findings show that Indians are managing present-day financial responsibilities relatively well, but long-term preparedness remains a challenge.

The India Health Quotient 2026 reveals that 80% of Indians acknowledge feeling stressed. Yet, most don't see stress as something overwhelming, with 69% describing it as manageable.
The findings point to a shift in how India views wellbeing. Mental health is no longer a secondary conversation. In fact, 75% prioritise mental health over social health when thinking about overall wellbeing.

India's Mental Health Quotient stands at 65/100, reflecting a population that is increasingly aware of its emotional wellbeing, while still navigating the pressures of modern life.
